title: Supernova remnants in the new radio astronomy era
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026(arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Ingallinera01
summary: Supernova remnants (SNRs) are what is left after stellar explosions, when the stellar ejecta, the explosion shock and the circumstellar medium interact. Despite being among the first objects studied in radio astronomy, observational difficulties have so far prevented a definitive characterisation, which would help answer open questions related to these sources. It is debated which is the contribution of SNRs to Galactic cosmic rays, or how the interaction with the surrounding environments influences the particle energetics. The SKA precursors are providing valuable and unexpected discoveries on SNRs, thanks to their unique capabilities to probe spatial scales from a few arcseconds to a few degrees with a sensitivity of tens of microjansky. Accurate integrated flux density measurements and arcsecond-scale spectral-index maps are now possible for tens of SNRs, substantially expanding the small subset of remnants traditionally studied in great detail. SKA will markedly enhance current observations by providing: higher sensitivity, enabling the detection of fainter SNRs also in polarisation, revealing diffuse structures and the underlying magnetic field configuration; higher angular resolution, allowing detailed mapping of compact remnants and reducing depolarisation in fine structures, tracing filaments and shocks fronts; wider frequency coverage to probe unexplored spectral windows, where spectral turnovers and breaks or cut-off may occur, establishing a direct connection to X-ray and γ-ray emission that constrains the electron population, and enabling accurate modelling of the non-thermal emission across the electromagnetic spectrum; improved image fidelity for more reliable cross-matching with other wavelengths, leading to a better understanding of the SNR-interstellar medium interplay.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews how SKA and its precursors enable high-sensitivity, high-resolution multi-frequency observations of supernova remnants (SNRs), addressing open questions about their contribution to Galactic cosmic rays and their interaction with the interstellar medium.
AI.motivation: Observational difficulties have prevented a definitive characterization of SNRs, leaving open questions about their contribution to Galactic cosmic rays and how their interaction with surrounding environments influences particle energetics.
AI.method: The paper synthesizes capabilities of SKA precursors (high sensitivity down to tens of microjansky, arcsecond-scale resolution, wide frequency coverage) and projects how SKA will enhance these with higher sensitivity for polarimetry, higher angular resolution for mapping compact structures and filaments, wider spectral coverage to detect turnovers and connect to X-ray/γ-ray emission, and improved image fidelity for multi-wavelength cross-matching.
AI.result: Accurate integrated flux density measurements and arcsecond-scale spectral-index maps are now possible for tens of SNRs, substantially expanding the small subset previously studied in detail. SKA will further enable detection of fainter SNRs in polarization, reveal diffuse structures and magnetic field configurations, trace filaments and shock fronts, and probe unexplored spectral windows.
AI.conclusion: SKA will markedly enhance current SNR observations, enabling accurate modeling of non-thermal emission across the electromagnetic spectrum and a better understanding of the SNR-interstellar medium interplay.

title: Search for Seeds of The Cradle of Stars: Study of The Evolution From Atomic to Molecular Hydrogen Clouds with 1000 AU Scale Resolution
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Yamamoto01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: The aim of this science case for SKA1-Mid is to elucidate the spatial and velocity structure of the Cold Neutral Medium (CNM) on scales below the Field length, thereby elucidating the physical processes that govern CNM structure formation and its role in the earliest stages of molecular cloud formation. This goal will be achieved through a unique observational combination of several-arcsecond angular resolution, high velocity resolution, and unprecedented surface-brightness sensitivity. These observations will reveal the characteristic size, morphology, velocity structure, and internal dynamics of CNM clumps, and will directly connect such structures to the earliest phases of the atomic to molecular transition. Full-polarization observations with SKA1-Mid will also enable emission-based Zeeman measurements of the CNM, allowing the magnetic field strength to be mapped and opening a new window on the role of magnetic fields in CNM formation and evolution. In particular, this will make it possible to determine whether magnetic fields primarily inhibit fragmentation by supporting the gas against compression, or instead guide anisotropic condensation and promote the development of small-scale CNM structure through thermal instability. In combination with interferometric spatial filtering and high spectral resolution, SKA1-Mid will selectively trace the CNM and robustly identify individual clumps in both position and velocity space. These capabilities will provide decisive tests of thermal instability and the two-phase turbulence model, and will establish a new observational foundation for understanding how molecular clouds emerge from the multi-phase atomic interstellar medium.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using SKA1-Mid to observe the Cold Neutral Medium (CNM) at high angular and velocity resolution to study its spatial and velocity structure below the Field length, aiming to understand CNM clump formation, the atomic-to-molecular transition, and the role of magnetic fields via Zeeman measurements, providing tests of thermal instability and two-phase turbulence models.
AI.motivation: To elucidate the spatial and velocity structure of the Cold Neutral Medium (CNM) on scales below the Field length, and to understand the physical processes governing CNM structure formation and its role in the earliest stages of molecular cloud formation.
AI.method: Observational combination of several-arcsecond angular resolution, high velocity resolution, and unprecedented surface-brightness sensitivity using SKA1-Mid; full-polarization observations for emission-based Zeeman measurements of magnetic field strength; interferometric spatial filtering and high spectral resolution to selectively trace CNM and identify individual clumps in position-velocity space.
AI.result: Will reveal characteristic size, morphology, velocity structure, and internal dynamics of CNM clumps; connect these structures to the earliest phases of the atomic-to-molecular transition; map magnetic field strength via Zeeman measurements; determine whether magnetic fields inhibit fragmentation or promote anisotropic condensation and small-scale CNM structure via thermal instability.
AI.conclusion: SKA1-Mid will provide decisive tests of thermal instability and the two-phase turbulence model, and establish a new observational foundation for understanding how molecular clouds emerge from the multi-phase atomic interstellar medium.

title: Transforming X-ray Binary Astrophysics with SKA+VLBI
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/TaoAn01
summary: X-ray binaries (XRBs) are unique laboratories where accretion, jets, strong gravity and magnetic fields can be probed on humanly tractable timescales. The phased SKA-Mid operating as a single, ultra-sensitive Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) element will transform radio studies of XRBs primarily through its time-domain capabilities: substantially improved sensitivity on VLBI baselines that include SKA-Mid in Bands 2 and 5, together with connected-element SKA-Mid imaging extending down to 0.35--1 GHz (Band 1), microarcsecond-precision astrometry for bright systems, high-fidelity polarimetry for the most strongly polarized sources, and rapid target-of-opportunity response. In synergy with global VLBI networks, SKA+VLBI will track the evolution of compact ejecta and compact jets on astronomical unit (AU) scales, measure frequency-dependent core shifts to infer magnetic field strengths and gradients, resolve disk--jet coupling during state transitions in real time, and determine precise distances and natal kicks via parallaxes and proper motions. Joint campaigns with future X-ray and optical telescopes will enable strictly simultaneous, multi-band constraints on accretion--ejection physics and on jet composition. We outline a quantitative program for \aastar\ and AA4, including cadenced, multi-frequency VLBI ``movies'' of jets over the first days of outbursts, an XRB astrometric census, and a core-shift survey, and we provide representative detection rates, magnetic field measurements and distance accuracies. These outcomes will set the microphysical foundation for jet physics across the mass scale from stellar-mass black holes and neutron stars to active galactic nuclei, and will establish SKA+VLBI as the definitive facility for time-domain, high-resolution XRB astrophysics.

AI.tldr: The paper outlines how SKA-Mid, operating as a VLBI element, will revolutionize X-ray binary studies through enhanced sensitivity, microarcsecond astrometry, high-fidelity polarimetry, and rapid response, enabling multi-frequency jet monitoring, core-shift surveys, and astrometric censuses that set the foundation for jet physics across mass scales.
AI.motivation: X-ray binaries provide unique laboratories for studying accretion, jets, strong gravity, and magnetic fields on humanly tractable timescales, making them ideal targets for transformative radio observations.
AI.method: SKA-Mid will operate as a single ultra-sensitive VLBI element in Bands 2 and 5, combined with connected-element SKA-Mid imaging (Band 1), global VLBI networks, and joint campaigns with X-ray/optical telescopes to enable time-domain, multi-frequency, polarimetric, and astrometric observations.
AI.result: The program will achieve AU-scale tracking of compact ejecta/jets, frequency-dependent core shifts for magnetic field inference, real-time disk-jet coupling during state transitions, and precise distances/natal kicks via parallaxes and proper motions, with representative detection rates, magnetic field measurements, and distance accuracies provided.
AI.conclusion: SKA+VLBI will establish the definitive facility for time-domain, high-resolution XRB astrophysics, setting the microphysical foundation for jet physics across mass scales from stellar-mass black holes/neutron stars to active galactic nuclei.

title: Extended Structure in E+A Galaxies Via Image Stacking
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures
summary: Small-scale interactions such as minor mergers, flybys and harassment are considered common driving mechanisms that can both initiate and quench star-forming processes within post-starburst (PSB) galaxies. PSBs have been linked to disturbed morphologies and faint tidal features in numerous works. We aim to independently study these features in E+A galaxies found in the Galaxy and Mass Assembly Fourth Data Release (GAMA DR4). Using image stacking techniques, we derive the averaged radial surface brightness profiles of E+A image stacks alongside the Sérsic parameters that best fit these profiles. These E+A stacks consist of 57 images extracted from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) in g, r & i bands. The E+A stacks are shown to have brighter extended regions than similar non-PSB galaxies, which is indicative of faint tidal features that could be caused by small-scale interactions. Additionally, we make use of Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Legacy Survey imaging, which is deeper than SDSS, to further support our conclusions and find that the Legacy Survey images independently strengthen the evidence for excess light at extended radii relative to the comparison samples. We discuss these findings in the context of future surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) survey.

AI.tldr: This paper studies E+A (post-starburst) galaxies from GAMA DR4 using image stacking of 57 SDSS images. The stacked profiles show brighter extended regions compared to non-PSB galaxies, indicating faint tidal features from small-scale interactions. These findings are confirmed with deeper DESI Legacy Survey data and discussed in the context of future LSST surveys.
AI.motivation: To independently study faint tidal features and disturbed morphologies in E+A (post-starburst) galaxies, which have been linked to small-scale interactions (minor mergers, flybys, harassment) that can initiate or quench star formation.
AI.method: Image stacking of 57 E+A galaxy images from SDSS (g, r, & i bands) extracted from GAMA DR4, derivation of averaged radial surface brightness profiles, fitting of Sérsic parameters, and validation using deeper DESI Legacy Survey imaging.
AI.result: E+A stacks exhibit brighter extended regions than comparable non-PSB galaxies, indicative of faint tidal features likely caused by small-scale interactions. DESI Legacy Survey data independently strengthens evidence for excess light at extended radii.
AI.conclusion: Small-scale interactions are common driving mechanisms for the post-starburst phase in E+A galaxies. The findings are discussed in the context of future deep surveys like LSST, which will enable even more detailed studies of these faint tidal features.

title: Unraveling the mysteries of supernovae with SKA+VLBI
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/TaoAn02
summary: Supernovae (SNe) drive cosmic chemical enrichment and shape galactic feedback, yet the link between progenitors and explosion outcomes remains poorly constrained because the earliest phases are rarely resolved. Radio emission traces synchrotron radiation where the fastest ejecta interact with the circumstellar medium (CSM), providing a uniquely penetrating probe of these phases. SKA-Mid phased into global VLBI will move from simple detections to routine interferometric imaging of nearby extragalactic SNe. Sub-$μ$Jy sensitivity and mas-scale SKA+VLBI imaging, complemented by visibility-domain model fitting for sub-beam radius measurements at 5-15 GHz will allow us to follow the expanding shocks of stripped-envelope SNe out to $\sim$25 Mpc, measure deceleration indices ($m$) and axial ratios to $\approx 5-10\%$, and directly test jet-assisted versus neutrino-driven explosion mechanisms. For interacting SNe (Type IIn/Ibn), SKA+VLBI will resolve clumpy and toroidal CSM on progenitor scales, constraining the timing and geometry of eruptive pre-explosion mass loss. Deep limits on Type Ia SNe will tightly restrict the allowed single-degenerate parameter space, while late-time imaging will search for nascent compact remnants and pulsar wind nebulae. In synergy with optical, X-ray and gravitational wave facilities, SKA+VLBI will turn nearby SNe into laboratories for time-resolved shock physics and progenitor mapping.

AI.tldr: This paper outlines how SKA-Mid phased into global VLBI, with sub-μJy sensitivity and mas-scale imaging at 5-15 GHz, will revolutionize supernova studies by resolving expanding shocks, measuring deceleration indices and axial ratios to 5-10%, testing explosion mechanisms, mapping circumstellar medium on progenitor scales, constraining Type Ia progenitor models, and searching for compact remnants, enabling time-resolved shock physics and progenitor mapping for nearby extragalactic SNe out to ~25 Mpc.
AI.motivation: The link between supernova progenitors and explosion outcomes is poorly constrained because the earliest phases are rarely resolved; radio emission uniquely penetrates these phases by tracing synchrotron radiation from ejecta–CSM interaction.
AI.method: SKA-Mid phased into global VLBI for sub-μJy sensitivity and mas-scale interferometric imaging at 5–15 GHz, complemented by visibility-domain model fitting for sub-beam radius measurements.
AI.result: Will track expanding shocks of stripped-envelope SNe to ~25 Mpc, measure m and axial ratios to ~5-10%; resolve clumpy/toroidal CSM on progenitor scales for interacting SNe; set deep limits on Type Ia single-degenerate parameter space; search for compact remnants and pulsar wind nebulae at late times.
AI.conclusion: SKA+VLBI, in synergy with optical, X-ray and gravitational wave facilities, will transform nearby SNe into laboratories for time-resolved shock physics and progenitor mapping.

title: SKA VLBI survey of the Southern sky for astrometry, geodesy, and astrophysics
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/MingHuiXu01
summary: The development of SKA will open the opportunity to run dedicated VLBI surveys of the Southern sky and observe sources not visible at radio telescopes located in the Northern hemisphere. These surveys will allow for doing geodesy with a Southern hemisphere-centered network, increase the density of compact radio sources that can be used as calibrators, further extend the celestial reference frame to deep south, and facilitate high-precision differential astrometry for a wide range of applications. Achieving a deep completeness level and determining the parsec-scale properties of extragalactic radio sources is crucial for multi-wavelength and multi-messenger astrophysics. This includes supporting Cherenkov and neutrino telescope science cases, as well as joint VLBI-Gaia studies of active galaxies.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses how the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will enable dedicated VLBI surveys of the Southern sky, supporting geodesy, celestial reference frame extension, calibrator density increase, and high-precision differential astrometry. These surveys are crucial for multi-wavelength and multi-messenger astrophysics, including Cherenkov/neutrino telescopes and VLBI-Gaia studies.
AI.motivation: To leverage SKA's capabilities for dedicated VLBI surveys of the Southern sky, addressing the lack of Southern hemisphere coverage in existing radio observations and enabling new geodetic, astrometric, and multi-messenger science.
AI.method: Conducting dedicated VLBI surveys using SKA to observe Southern sky sources, focusing on achieving deep completeness and determining parsec-scale properties of extragalactic radio sources.
AI.result: Surveys will enable geodetic measurements with a Southern hemisphere-centered network, increase calibrator density, extend the celestial reference frame southward, and facilitate high-precision differential astrometry.
AI.conclusion: SKA-driven Southern VLBI surveys are essential for advancing multi-wavelength and multi-messenger astrophysics, supporting Cherenkov/neutrino telescope science, and enabling joint VLBI-Gaia studies of active galaxies.

title: Broad-band Spectral Modeling of Large-Scale X-ray Jets in High-Redshift Quasars: An MHD-Informed Approach
comment: Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a systematic spectral analysis of kiloparsec-scale jets in high-redshift quasars, modeling their radio-to-X-ray emission as synchrotron radiation and inverse-comptonization of CMB by relativistic electrons. In contrast to the homogeneous one-zone approximation commonly adopted in the literature, we describe the jet as a current-carrying, axially symmetric outflow with a purely toroidal magnetic field in magnetohydrostatic equilibrium and with radial velocity shear. In this framework, the pressure, magnetic-field, and bulk-velocity profiles are linked self-consistently, capturing the radial stratification of the emitting region without introducing additional free parameters. For any individual source, the model effectively retains only a small number of free parameters, including the total jet power, $L_{\rm j}$, and the on-axis bulk Lorentz factor, $Γ_0$. We consider two prescriptions for the radial distribution of the radiating electrons -- proportional either to the gas pressure or to the rest-frame magnetic energy density -- and two toroidal-field profiles, yielding four model variants. Applying the model to a sample of ten quasar jets at $z \geq 2.5$ with X-ray features resolved by \textit{Chandra}, we perform Bayesian parameter inference and model comparison. The Bayesian evidence systematically favors electron distributions that follow the gas pressure rather than the magnetic energy density, while the data discriminate only weakly between the assumed field profiles. The inferred jet powers, reaching $L_{\rm j} \sim 10^{49}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, are systematically larger than those obtained from one-zone models, and the corresponding global jet magnetization parameters are low. None of the derived quantities, including $Γ_0 \sim \mathcal{O}(10)$, shows a significant monotonic trend with redshift.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a stratified jet model for kiloparsec-scale quasar jets at high redshift, using Bayesian inference on ten sources to show that electron distributions tracing gas pressure are favored over magnetic energy density, and that derived jet powers (~10^49 erg/s) are higher than one-zone approximations, with no redshift evolution of key parameters.
AI.motivation: To improve upon the homogeneous one-zone approximation commonly used to model radio-to-X-ray emission from high-redshift quasar jets by introducing a physically self-consistent, radially stratified jet model that links pressure, magnetic-field, and bulk-velocity profiles without extra free parameters.
AI.method: A systematic spectral analysis of kiloparsec-scale jets in ten quasars at z ≥ 2.5, modeling emission as synchrotron + inverse-Compton of CMB. The jet is described as a current-carrying, axially symmetric outflow with purely toroidal magnetic field in magnetohydrostatic equilibrium and radial velocity shear. Four model variants combine two electron distribution prescriptions (gas pressure vs. magnetic energy density) and two toroidal-field profiles. Bayesian parameter inference and model comparison are performed.
AI.result: Bayesian evidence systematically favors electron distributions following gas pressure over magnetic energy density. Inferred jet powers (L_j ~ 10^49 erg/s) are systematically larger than one-zone models, global magnetization is low, and derived quantities including Γ_0 ~ O(10) show no significant monotonic redshift trend.
AI.conclusion: A stratified jet model is more physically realistic than one-zone approximations and yields systematically higher jet powers; the data favor pressure-tracking electron distributions, while field profile choices are less constrained. No redshift evolution of jet parameters is detected.

title: NO molecule in massive star forming regions
summary: Context. Among diatomic molecules composed of the abundant elements C, N and O, NO has been detected far less than the well studied CN and CO, making it a crucial yet under-observed component in nitrogen-containing chemical networks. NO was thought to serve as a potential tracer of shocks, as evidenced with orders abundance enhancements reported in literature. Aims. Large-sample observations for NO molecule in widespread interstellar environments are needed to confirm if the enhancement of NO is due to shock chemistry or not. Methods. Single-point survey for NO lines around 150 GHz was carried out by Arizona Radio Observatory 12-meter telescope towards a sample of 36 massive star forming regions containing SiO emission, which include three evolutionary stages: 4 IRDCs, 6 protostars and 26 H II regions. Results. The NO emission was detected in 28 sources with a detection rate of 78%. Beam-averaged NO column densities and abundances relative to H2 were derived from integrated intensities of two main hyperfine lines. Correlations between NO and SiO in integrated intensity and relative abundance are similar to the corresponding correlations of c-C3H2, indicating that NO enrichment may not significantly involve pronounced shock activities, which coincides with the trend in line widths: NO is close to c-C3H2, both smaller than H2CO and far smaller than SiO. Conclusions. Observational evidence does not strongly support significant NO enhancement by shock chemistry in the observed sources, indicating that the formation of NO does not necessarily require shocks.

AI.tldr: A survey of NO emission toward 36 massive star-forming regions (78% detection rate) finds that NO abundances do not strongly correlate with shock tracers like SiO, suggesting NO formation does not necessarily require shocks, contrary to previous assumptions.
AI.motivation: NO has been under-observed compared to CN and CO among C, N, O diatomic molecules. It was thought to be a shock tracer based on earlier abundance enhancement reports, but large-sample observations across diverse environments were lacking to confirm this.
AI.method: Single-point survey of NO lines at ~150 GHz using the Arizona Radio Observatory 12-meter telescope toward 36 massive star-forming regions with SiO emission, spanning three evolutionary stages: 4 IRDCs, 6 protostars, and 26 H II regions. Beam-averaged NO column densities and abundances relative to H2 derived from integrated intensities of two main hyperfine lines.
AI.result: NO detected in 28/36 sources (78% detection rate). Correlations between NO and SiO in integrated intensity and relative abundance resemble those of c-C3H2, not the shock tracer SiO. NO line widths are close to c-C3H2, smaller than H2CO and much smaller than SiO.
AI.conclusion: Observational evidence does not strongly support significant NO enhancement by shock chemistry; NO formation does not necessarily require shocks.

title: Exploring Tidal Disruption Events with SKA and VLBI: Unveiling the Mystery of Black Hole Feeding and Outflows
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Shu01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) probe the birth and evolution of black hole accretion flows and jets on human timescales. Radio emission traces shocks and outflows from thermal TDEs and powerful relativistic jets in the rare jetted class. SKA Mid, phased for VLBI and used together with global networks, will deliver milliarcsecond imaging, tens of microarcsecond astrometry, and microJy sensitivity, enabling: (i) proper motion measurements that discriminate off axis relativistic jets from subrelativistic winds; (ii) resolved morphologies and magnetic field diagnostics via polarimetry; and (iii) precise nuclear localization to distinguish SMBH vs. IMBH and to reveal recoiling or binary systems. SKA's wide frequency coverage (0.35 to 15.4 GHz) and 1h continuum sensitivities of 3 to 10 microJy per beam, together with multibeam tiedarray VLBI and a transient buffer for rapid triggers, are transformational. LSST, Einstein Probe, and SVOM will increase TDE alerts to hundreds per year, and late time radio flares appear common, ensuring rich SKA VLBI samples. We provide observing strategies, detection forecasts, and predictions, e.g., about 5 proper motion detections of jetted (or off axis) TDEs per year and routine core shift constraints at the microarcsecond level. This program will establish TDEs as laboratories for exploring jet launching, particle acceleration (including neutrinos), black hole accretion history and demographics, and properties of circumnuclear medium.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that SKA Mid, combined with VLBI capabilities, will revolutionize TDE studies by enabling microarcsecond astrometry, microJy sensitivity, and wide frequency coverage to probe jet launching, proper motions, magnetic fields, and black hole demographics, with forecasts of ~5 proper motion detections per year and routine core shift measurements.
AI.motivation: TDEs probe black hole accretion and jet evolution on human timescales, but current radio observations lack the angular resolution, sensitivity, and sample size to robustly discriminate between jet and wind models, measure proper motions, or localize events precisely. The upcoming SKA era with LSST, Einstein Probe, and SVOM will yield hundreds of TDE alerts per year, motivating the need for transformative radio capabilities.
AI.method: The paper outlines observing strategies using SKA Mid (0.35–15.4 GHz) with phased-array VLBI, multibeam tied-array mode, and a transient buffer for rapid triggering. It leverages milliarcsecond imaging, tens of microarcsecond astrometry, and microJy continuum sensitivity (3–10 µJy/beam in 1h) to conduct proper motion measurements, polarimetry for magnetic field diagnostics, and nuclear localization for SMBH/IMBH discrimination and binary/recoil detection.
AI.result: The paper forecasts ~5 proper motion detections per year for jetted (or off-axis) TDEs, routine core-shift constraints at the microarcsecond level, resolved morphological and polarimetric diagnostics, and precise nuclear localization. The increased TDE discovery rate (hundreds per year) and prevalence of late-time radio flares ensure a rich VLBI sample.
AI.conclusion: The SKA VLBI program will establish TDEs as laboratories for studying jet launching, particle acceleration (including neutrino production), black hole accretion history and demographics, and circumnuclear medium properties, transforming TDEs from rare events into systematic probes of supermassive black hole physics.

title: Semi-empirical Predictions for Ultra-deep Radio Counts of Star-forming Galaxies with the SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026(arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Giulietti01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Star-forming galaxies (SFGs) dominate the faint radio sky at flux densities below 0.1 mJy. Identifying these systems through a multiwavelength approach is essential to tracing the cosmic history of star formation. Upcoming surveys with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) in its AA4 configuration for the Mid array will probe these faint populations, offering unprecedented insights into the star formation activity of galaxies across cosmic time. Semi-empirical models, built on minimal assumptions and empirical galaxy relations, provide an efficient framework to study galaxy evolution using recent radio and optical/near-infrared (NIR) data. We developed SEMPER (Semi-EMPirical model for Extragalactic Radio emission) to predict the radio luminosity functions and number counts of SFGs. SEMPER combines redshift-dependent stellar mass functions from deep NIR surveys with empirical relations such as the galaxy main sequence and the IR/radio correlation, to characterise the radio properties of massive, high-redshift galaxies. The model shows excellent agreement with recent deep radio observations and naturally predicts a substantial population of massive, dust-obscured galaxies already in place at early epochs. In this chapter, we extend the SEMPER framework to SKA surveys by including an evolving starburst fraction and computing differential number counts at 1.4 GHz for both lensed and unlensed SFGs. Furthermore, we predict the cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) traced by radio-emitting galaxies up to $z\approx10$. Our results show that SKA surveys will probe the faintest flux-density regimes, dominated by galaxies powered by star formation, and that <20 hours of SKA-Mid Band 2 observations will recover at least $\approx$20% of the total SFRD predicted by SEMPER, including contributions from optically/NIR-dark systems up to $z\approx 6$.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SEMPER, a semi-empirical model predicting radio emission from star-forming galaxies, and shows that SKA-Mid surveys with <20 hours of observations will recover ~20% of the cosmic star formation rate density up to z≈6, including optically/NIR-dark galaxies.
AI.motivation: To develop a predictive framework for understanding the radio properties of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and their cosmic star formation history, leveraging upcoming deep SKA surveys that will probe faint radio populations below 0.1 mJy.
AI.method: Built SEMPER (Semi-EMPirical model for Extragalactic Radio emission), combining redshift-dependent stellar mass functions from deep NIR surveys with empirical relations (galaxy main sequence, IR/radio correlation). Extended the model to include an evolving starburst fraction and computed differential number counts at 1.4 GHz for both lensed and unlensed SFGs.
AI.result: SEMPER agrees well with deep radio observations and predicts a substantial population of massive, dust-obscured galaxies at early epochs. SKA surveys will probe the faintest flux-density regimes, and <20 hours of SKA-Mid Band 2 observations will recover at least ~20% of the total SFRD predicted by SEMPER, including contributions from optically/NIR-dark systems up to z≈6.
AI.conclusion: SKA surveys will provide unprecedented constraints on the star formation history of galaxies, particularly for faint, dust-obscured populations at high redshift, and SEMPER offers a robust framework for interpreting these observations.

title: Gamma-ray Bursts and Kilonovae from Gravitational Wave Events
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Colombo01
summary: The detection of gravitational waves (GWs) from binary black holes in 2015 and the joint GW-electromagnetic (EM) observation of the binary neutron star merger GW170817 set a milestone in the multimessenger era in astrophysics. After four observing runs by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA interferometers, a new cycle is planned for 2028, paving the way for next-generation detectors in the 2030s -- such as the Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer, and LISA. The prospects for joint GW-EM studies, including kilonova searches in wide optical surveys, are vast but demanding. In the radio domain, connected interferometers and VLBI arrays have already proven essential in constraining the ejecta properties of GW170817. Radio emission from gamma-ray burst (GRB) afterglows, whether on- or off-axis, remains detectable for very long time, making radio observations the most effective method for identifying and tracking GW merger counterparts. These observations enable precise characterization of system evolution, detailed probing of GRB jet structures, and possible detection of misaligned jets once their velocity becomes non-relativistic. Even in its initial configuration (AA*), the SKAO will provide the sensitivity and field of view needed to complement GW counterpart searches during O5 and beyond, offering unmatched capabilities for long-term monitoring. Furthermore, independent of the GW detections, SKAO will enable population studies of the properties of both long (produced by the collapse of massive stars) and short (produced by the merger of neutron stars) GRBs, of their jets and of their environment. We present an overview of this evolving observational landscape and of the key scientific questions SKAO will address.

AI.tldr: This paper outlines the current and future landscape of multimessenger astrophysics with gravitational waves and electromagnetic observations, focusing on the role of the SKAO in detecting and studying GW merger counterparts, particularly through radio observations of GRB afterglows and kilonovae.
AI.motivation: To assess the scientific capabilities and key questions the SKAO will address in the emerging multimessenger era, following the milestone GW detections by LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA and the joint GW-EM observation of GW170817.
AI.method: The paper provides an overview of the observational landscape, reviewing the use of connected interferometers and VLBI arrays for constraining ejecta properties, and projecting the SKAO's sensitivity and field of view for GW counterpart searches during O5 and beyond.
AI.result: Radio observations are the most effective method for identifying and tracking GW merger counterparts due to long-detectable GRB afterglow emission. The SKAO in its AA* initial configuration will provide unmatched capabilities for long-term monitoring and complement GW counterpart searches.
AI.conclusion: The SKAO will enable population studies of long and short GRBs, their jets and environments, and will be instrumental for joint GW-EM studies, independent of GW detections.

title: Validating the ICCF-Cut Method with Simultaneous Photometric and Spectroscopic H$α$ Reverberation Mapping of NGC 4151 and UGC 3374
comment: 24 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Photometric reverberation mapping (RM) provides an efficient alternative to spectroscopic RM for probing the broad-line region (BLR) sizes in AGNs. In our previous work, we proposed the ICCF-Cut method, which extracts H$α$ emission-line variability from broadband photometric light curves and measures the lags to estimate the BLR sizes. To further assess the reliability of this method, we conduct simultaneous photometric and spectroscopic monitoring of two nearby Seyfert galaxies, NGC 4151 and UGC 3374, over multiple observing seasons using the Lijiang 2.4 m telescope. By directly comparing the photometric and spectroscopic RM results in each season, we find that the extracted H$α$ light curves using the ICCF-Cut method closely resemble those derived from spectroscopy. The photometric H$α$ lags are also generally consistent with the spectroscopic H$α$ lags within the uncertainties. For several seasons where the photometric H$α$ lags are slightly underestimated, we find that the discrepancy may be caused by residual He\,\textsc{i} contamination in the extracted H$α$ light curves. After correcting for this contamination, the photometric lag measurements become more consistent with the spectroscopic results. We further explore the performance of the ICCF-Cut method using the simulated light curves with different filter bandwidths. For our observational and simulated cases, the method can successfully recover the emission-line variability and lag measurements broadly consistent with the spectroscopic results. This provides further support for the applicability of the ICCF-Cut method in photometric RM.

AI.tldr: This paper validates the ICCF-Cut method for photometric reverberation mapping by comparing photometric and spectroscopic RM results for NGC 4151 and UGC 3374, finding consistent Hα lags after correcting for He I contamination, and further supporting the method with simulations.
AI.motivation: To assess the reliability of the ICCF-Cut method for extracting Hα emission-line variability from broadband photometric light curves for BLR size estimation in AGNs.
AI.method: Simultaneous photometric and spectroscopic monitoring of NGC 4151 and UGC 3374 over multiple seasons using the Lijiang 2.4 m telescope, comparing extracted Hα light curves and lags from both techniques, with additional simulations using different filter bandwidths.
AI.result: Photometric Hα light curves and lags are generally consistent with spectroscopic results; slight underestimation in some seasons is attributed to residual He I contamination, which when corrected yields better agreement.
AI.conclusion: The ICCF-Cut method can reliably recover emission-line variability and lag measurements consistent with spectroscopic RM, supporting its applicability for photometric RM.

title: Optical observations of candidate host galaxies of eight fast X-ray transients
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures and 5 tables. Version accepted by A&A
summary: Fast X-ray transients (FXTs) are extragalactic flashes of X-rays with a typical duration of minutes to hours for which a variety of origins has been proposed and observed. To decipher the origin of FXTs, particularly those lacking multi-wavelength counterparts, we aim to understand their energetics and environments. We present deep optical ground-based observations of the positions of eight FXTs in order to try and identify and characterize candidate host galaxies. We use their properties to discriminate between possible progenitor scenarios. We identify candidate host galaxies for Swift~J050400.2+673405, XRT140507, XRT040610, XRT151121, XRT191127 and EP240708a. For each candidate, we infer the spectroscopic or photometric redshift, stellar mass, star formation rate, metallicity and stellar population age by fitting our data with the spectral energy distribution fitting code BAGPIPES. We re-identify XRT191223 as a Galactic stellar flare. For several FXTs, there are multiple candidate host galaxies, which complicates deriving constraints on the origin of the FXT. Assuming association with (one of) those candidates, all are consistent with a (non-)relativistic white dwarf - intermediate mass black hole tidal disruption event (WD-IMBH TDE) and a binary neutron star (BNS) merger. Two are consistent with a supernova shock breakout and only EP240708a with cocoon emission from a long gamma-ray burst. We also discuss the possibility that the host galaxies remain undetected in our observations. We conclude that FXTs detected by Chandra and XMM-Newton are likely to arise from a variety of origins, and we discuss that part of this population differs from FXTs detected by Einstein Probe many of which appear consistent with a collapsar scenario.

AI.tldr: This paper presents deep optical observations of eight Fast X-ray Transients (FXTs) to identify and characterize their candidate host galaxies, finding that most FXTs are consistent with multiple progenitor scenarios (WD-IMBH tidal disruption events or binary neutron star mergers), while only a subset matches supernova shock breakout or GRB cocoon emission, concluding that FXTs detected by Chandra and XMM-Newton likely have diverse origins distinct from Einstein Probe-detected FXTs which often align with the collapsar scenario.
AI.motivation: To decipher the origin of extragalactic FXTs (especially those without multi-wavelength counterparts) by understanding their energetics and environments through host galaxy identification and characterization.
AI.method: Deep optical ground-based observations of eight FXT positions; SED fitting with BAGPIPES to infer photometric/spectroscopic redshifts, stellar masses, star formation rates, metallicities, and stellar population ages of candidate host galaxies.
AI.result: Candidate hosts identified for 6 FXTs; one (XRT191223) reclassified as Galactic stellar flare; multiple candidate hosts complicate origin constraints; all FXTs are consistent with WD-IMBH TDE and BNS merger scenarios; two consistent with supernova shock breakout; only EP240708a consistent with long GRB cocoon emission.
AI.conclusion: FXTs detected by Chandra and XMM-Newton likely arise from a variety of origins and differ from Einstein Probe-detected FXTs, many of which appear consistent with a collapsar scenario.

title: Feeding and Feedback in Dwarf Galaxies (FeeD) -- I. Evidence of nuclear ultra-fast and galaxy-scale outflows in the dwarf galaxy Arp 151
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, Accepted for publication in A&A Letters
summary: Feeding and feedback regulated by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) play a central role in galaxy growth and evolution, yet these processes remain poorly understood in low-mass galaxies. In particular, the presence, properties, and role of ultra-fast nuclear outflows (UFOs) in low-mass galaxy systems are largely unexplored. We analyze available NuSTAR X-ray observations of Arp 151 and find a possible evidence ($\sim 2σ$ confidence) for a fast outflow with a velocity of $\sim0.18c$ from the central BH. Furthermore, we have also detected an optical galaxy-scale outflow in MaNGA Integral Field Unit data. The estimated nuclear and galaxy-scale mass outflow rates are $\sim0.015$ $M_\odot$/yr from {\it NuSTAR} and $\sim0.43$ $M_\odot$/yr from MaNGA, respectively. Our estimates suggest that such outflows may significantly regulate the feedback process in the galaxy. Comparing the kinetics of the UFO and the galaxy-scale outflow indicates that they are in the momentum-conserving phase. This tentative detection implies that dwarf galaxies are also able to generate UFOs, which so far have been detected in massive galaxies. Thus, the AGN feedback may also be important for the evolution of the dwarf galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents tentative evidence (∼2σ) for an ultra-fast outflow (UFO) with velocity ∼0.18c in the low-mass galaxy Arp 151 using NuSTAR X-ray data, alongside a detected galaxy-scale optical outflow from MaNGA. The nuclear and galaxy-scale mass outflow rates are ∼0.015 M⊙/yr and ∼0.43 M⊙/yr, respectively, suggesting these outflows may significantly regulate feedback. The outflows appear momentum-conserving, indicating that dwarf galaxies can host UFOs and AGN feedback may be important for dwarf galaxy evolution.
AI.motivation: To explore the presence, properties, and role of ultra-fast nuclear outflows (UFOs) in low-mass galaxies, which remain largely unexplored despite the well-known role of SMBH feedback in massive galaxies.
AI.method: Analysis of NuSTAR X-ray observations of Arp 151 for evidence of UFOs, combined with MaNGA Integral Field Unit data to detect and characterize galaxy-scale optical outflows.
AI.result: Tentative detection (∼2σ) of a UFO with velocity ∼0.18c; nuclear mass outflow rate ∼0.015 M⊙/yr from NuSTAR; galaxy-scale outflow rate ∼0.43 M⊙/yr from MaNGA; the kinematics suggest the outflows are in a momentum-conserving phase.
AI.conclusion: Dwarf galaxies can generate UFOs (previously only detected in massive galaxies), implying that AGN feedback may also play an important role in the evolution of low-mass galaxies.

title: Stellar black hole binaries from two common envelope evolution phases in triple stellar systems
comment: It will be submitted in two days to allow for comments (including missing references)
summary: We propose a triple-star evolutionary channel involving two common envelope evolution (CEE) phases to form close binary black hole (BBH) systems with an average positive effective inspiral spin $χ_{\rm eff}$ and a tail of systems having $χ_{\rm eff}<0$, as observed by gravitational wave detectors. $χ_{\rm eff}$ is the mass-weighted spin of the two merging BHs, and a positive (negative) value is for an effective spin along (opposite) the orbital angular momentum. The first BH progenitor engulfs a low-mass star during the post-main-sequence evolution. The tertiary star spirals in and spins up the core, which forms the first BH at the first core-collapse supernova (CCSN) explosion. Its spin is along the orbital angular momentum of the inner binary, which can be highly inclined to the outer binary angular momentum. The secondary star later engulfs the BH in a second CEE phase and explodes as a CCSN to form the second BH with a spin that is more aligned with the orbital angular momentum of the two BHs. We use empirically calibrated initial distributions of triple-star systems consisting of two massive stars and impose a hierarchical stability criterion. We compare the predicted ratio of merging BBHs to CCSN explosion rates and find it is up to a factor of 2 larger than the observed rate. This channel can significantly contribute to the population of observed merging BBHs and can explain their qualitative spin distribution.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a triple-star evolutionary channel with two common envelope phases to form close binary black hole (BBH) systems. This channel can produce merging BBHs with positive effective inspiral spin (χeff) and a tail of negative χeff systems, matching gravitational wave observations. The predicted merger rate can be up to ~2× the observed rate, suggesting this channel significantly contributes to the observed BBH population and explains their spin distribution.
AI.motivation: To explain the observed distribution of effective inspiral spin (χeff) in merging binary black hole (BBH) systems detected by gravitational wave observatories, specifically the prevalence of positive χeff values with a tail of negative values, which standard binary evolution channels struggle to reproduce.
AI.method: The authors propose a triple-star evolutionary channel involving two successive common envelope evolution (CEE) phases. In the first CEE, a tertiary star spirals into a post-main-sequence primary, spinning up its core to produce a first BH with spin aligned with the inner binary's orbital angular momentum (which can be highly inclined relative to the outer orbit). In the second CEE, the secondary star engulfs the first BH and later explodes as a core-collapse supernova to form the second BH with a spin more aligned with the final binary's orbital angular momentum. The model uses empirically calibrated initial distributions of triple-star systems with two massive stars and imposes a hierarchical stability criterion.
AI.result: The predicted ratio of merging BBHs to core-collapse supernova explosion rates is up to a factor of 2 larger than the observed rate. This channel can significantly contribute to the observed population of merging BBHs and explains the qualitative spin distribution (average positive χeff with a tail of negative values).
AI.conclusion: The triple-star evolutionary channel with two common envelope phases is a viable and potentially dominant formation pathway for merging BBH systems observed by gravitational wave detectors, particularly in explaining their spin distributions.

title: Probing outflow physics through CH$_3$CN and CH$_3$OH chemistry
summary: Chemical correlations between molecules provide powerful diagnostics to probe the physical conditions of protostellar outflows. In particular, the relationship between methanol (CH$_3$OH) and methyl cyanide (CH$_3$CN) offers a promising tool to investigate the chemistry and irradiation environment of shocked gas. In this Letter, we use the CH$_3$OH/CH$_3$CN abundance ratio to constrain the physical properties of the outflow driven by the Class 0 protostar S68N using ALMA Band 3 and Band 6 observations. Assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), we derive excitation temperatures of 50-60 K and column densities of 2-3$\times$10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$ for CH$_3$CN and 3-5$\times$10$^{15}$ cm$^{-2}$ for CH$_3$OH. The resulting CH$_3$OH/CH$_3$CN abundance ratio is nearly constant along the outflow, with values of $\sim$100-200, similar to those found in other protostellar environments. Using an up-to-date astrochemical model, we test whether gas-phase formation of CH$_3$CN can account for the observed ratios. We find that they are reproduced only by assuming enhanced cosmic-ray ionization rates $ζ_{\rm CR}$ up to $\sim$10$^{-14}$ s$^{-1}$. These results suggest that the CH$_3$OH-CH$_3$CN correlation can be used as a probe of the irradiation conditions in protostellar outflows. Further studies are required to explore the possible contribution of grain-surface formation of CH$_3$CN which could lead to a lower $ζ_{\rm CR}$ and to extend the analysis to a larger sample of sources.

AI.tldr: Using ALMA observations and astrochemical modeling, the study derives CH₃OH/CH₃CN abundance ratios (~100-200) in the S68N protostellar outflow and finds they can be explained by enhanced cosmic-ray ionization rates (~10⁻¹⁴ s⁻¹), suggesting this molecular ratio probes irradiation conditions in shocked gas.
AI.motivation: Chemical correlations between molecules, specifically the CH₃OH/CH₃CN abundance ratio, offer a promising diagnostic to probe the physical conditions (chemistry and irradiation environment) of protostellar outflows.
AI.method: ALMA Band 3 and Band 6 observations of the Class 0 protostar S68N outflow; LTE analysis to derive excitation temperatures (50-60 K) and column densities for CH₃CN (2-3×10¹³ cm⁻²) and CH₃OH (3-5×10¹⁵ cm⁻²); comparison with up-to-date astrochemical models testing gas-phase CH₃CN formation under varying cosmic-ray ionization rates.
AI.result: CH₃OH/CH₃CN abundance ratio is nearly constant along the outflow (~100-200), similar to other protostellar environments. Observed ratios are reproduced only when assuming enhanced cosmic-ray ionization rates ζ_CR up to ~10⁻¹⁴ s⁻¹.
AI.conclusion: The CH₃OH–CH₃CN correlation can be used as a probe of irradiation conditions in protostellar outflows. Further studies are needed to investigate grain-surface CH₃CN formation, which could imply lower ζ_CR, and to extend analysis to a larger source sample.

title: A search for Fast Radio Bursts from globular clusters in M49 with FAST
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The origins of fast radio bursts (FRBs) remain uncertain, although magnetars are a leading progenitor candidate. Because magnetars are thought to form primarily through core-collapse supernovae in young stellar populations, the discovery of FRB 20200120E in a globular cluster (GC) in the nearby galaxy M81 was unexpected given the ancient stellar populations of GCs. Expanding the sample of FRBs localised to nearby galaxies is therefore essential for testing FRB formation channels in old stellar environments. M49 (NGC 4472) is a nearby (~17 Mpc), radio-quiet giant elliptical galaxy in the Virgo cluster hosting about 7000 GCs, making it an ideal target for GC FRB searches. We conducted a 9-hour SnapShotCal observation of M49 using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST) 19-beam receiver, covering approximately 4230 GCs (2.1 hr per GC), and performed a comprehensive single-pulse search over a dispersion measure range of 0-5000 pc cm^-3. No unambiguous astrophysical FRBs were detected. The most significant trigger reached a post-processed signal-to-noise ratio of 8.6 sigma at a dispersion measure of 412.2 pc cm^-3, but is statistically consistent with thermal noise after accounting for the false-alarm rate. We derive a beam-averaged peak flux-density sensitivity of about 16.5 mJy (corresponding to a fluence limit of about 16.5 mJy ms for a 1 ms burst) and place an upper limit on the FRB occurrence rate of 4.7 x 10^-4 FRB GC^-1 hr^-1. Our non-detection constrains only bright bursts above this fluence threshold during the observing window.

AI.tldr: A 9-hour FAST observation of M49 (NGC 4472) targeting ~4230 globular clusters for FRB detection yielded no unambiguous astrophysical FRBs. The study places an upper limit on the FRB occurrence rate of 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ FRB GC⁻¹ hr⁻¹ above a fluence threshold of ~16.5 mJy ms, constraining bright burst rates in old stellar populations.
AI.motivation: The discovery of FRB 20200120E in a globular cluster (old stellar population) challenged the prevailing magnetar-core-collapse supernova paradigm. Expanding the sample of FRBs localized to nearby galaxies is essential for testing FRB formation channels in old stellar environments.
AI.method: 9-hour SnapShotCal observation using FAST 19-beam receiver targeting M49 (giant elliptical galaxy in Virgo cluster, ~17 Mpc) covering ~4230 globular clusters (2.1 hr per GC). Comprehensive single-pulse search over DM range 0-5000 pc cm⁻³.
AI.result: No unambiguous astrophysical FRBs detected. Most significant trigger: SNR 8.6σ at DM 412.2 pc cm⁻³, consistent with thermal noise. Beam-averaged peak flux-density sensitivity ~16.5 mJy (fluence limit ~16.5 mJy ms for 1 ms burst). Upper limit on FRB occurrence rate: 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ FRB GC⁻¹ hr⁻¹.
AI.conclusion: The non-detection constrains only bright bursts above the fluence threshold during the observing window, providing a null result for FRB rates in M49's globular cluster system.

title: Theoretical determination of the binding energies of methanol and related species onto amorphous solid water ice
comment: Resubmitted to AAS Journals following revision
summary: The formation and survival of complex organic molecules (COMs) in cold interstellar environments depends on their interactions with icy dust grain surfaces. Methanol, a key COM detected in cold cores and protoplanetary disks, is believed to form on amorphous solid water (ASW) through surface reactions and reside there until it is desorbed into the gas phase. We present a theoretical study of the binding energies (BEs) of methanol and its photolysis-derived species on ASW clusters by means of dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT) using a refined protocol implemented in the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP). Molecules capable of hydrogen bonding, such as H2O, CH3OH, HCOOH, and OH, exhibit high BEs and broad BE distributions that reflect the structural heterogeneity of the ASW surface. In contrast, weakly interacting volatiles including CO, CO2, CH4, and CH3 display narrower distributions dominated by dispersion interactions. Open-shell radicals such as CH2OH and OH bind more strongly than HCO and CH3 due to their ability to form directional hydrogen bonds. Incorporation of our BEs into an astrochemical model, in conjunction with a recalculation of the pre-exponential factor using transition state theory, demonstrates the sensitivity of model results to the method of calculation of the grain-surface reaction rates. The new approach generally predicts a higher abundance of radicals on the ice that are key reactants for the formation of COMs when surface diffusion is assumed to be efficient. These findings emphasize the importance of incorporating BEs that have been determined in a self-consistent manner into astrochemical models, and provide reliable theoretical benchmarks for species with limited experimental data.

AI.tldr: This study uses DFT calculations to determine binding energies of methanol and its photolysis-derived species on amorphous solid water, revealing that hydrogen-bonding species have high and broad BE distributions while weakly interacting volatiles have narrow distributions. Incorporating these self-consistent BEs into astrochemical models significantly affects predicted abundances of radicals and COMs.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation and survival of complex organic molecules (COMs) in cold interstellar environments, which depends on their interactions with icy dust grain surfaces, and to address the need for reliable, self-consistent binding energies for astrochemical modeling.
AI.method: Dispersion-corrected DFT using a refined protocol implemented in the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) on ASW clusters, coupled with astrochemical modeling incorporating transition state theory for pre-exponential factor recalculation.
AI.result: Hydrogen-bonding species (H2O, CH3OH, HCOOH, OH) show high BEs with broad distributions; weakly interacting volatiles (CO, CO2, CH4, CH3) show narrow dispersion-dominated distributions; open-shell radicals (CH2OH, OH) bind more strongly than HCO and CH3. The new BE approach predicts higher radical abundances on ice when surface diffusion is efficient.
AI.conclusion: Self-consistent determination of binding energies is critical for accurate astrochemical modeling of COM formation, and the calculated BEs provide reliable theoretical benchmarks for species with limited experimental data.

title: Origins of Cosmic Rays in the Galactic-extragalactic Transition Energy Range
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Corstanje01
summary: Cosmic rays arrive at Earth with energies ranging from $10^9$ to over $10^{20}$ eV. One of the open questions in high-energy cosmic ray science concerns the origin of the highest-energy cosmic rays that can be accelerated by Galactic sources, and the transition energy beyond which only extragalactic sources can provide. Measuring the mass composition gives essential information for comparing measurements to source and propagation models, both from the abundances at the source and from the maximum attainable energy which is proportional to the particle charge (and hence its mass). The highest-energy cosmic rays from the Galaxy are found in a range of $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ eV which is well suited for radio detection. Building on a decade of experience in measuring cosmic rays at LOFAR, we show that SKA-Low, augmented with an array of small particle detectors, is well suited to advance the field by measuring the mass composition of cosmic rays across this energy range.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that SKA-Low, enhanced with small particle detectors, can measure the mass composition of cosmic rays in the 10^16 to 10^18 eV range, addressing the transition between Galactic and extragalactic cosmic ray sources by building on LOFAR's decade of experience in radio detection.
AI.motivation: To address the open question of the origin of the highest-energy Galactic cosmic rays and the transition energy to extragalactic sources, by measuring the mass composition of cosmic rays, which provides essential information on source abundances and maximum attainable energy.
AI.method: Radio detection of cosmic rays using SKA-Low augmented with an array of small particle detectors, building on a decade of experience from LOFAR measurements.
AI.result: SKA-Low, when augmented with small particle detectors, is well suited to advance the field of cosmic ray mass composition measurements in the 10^16 to 10^18 eV energy range.
AI.conclusion: The SKA-Low array, enhanced with particle detectors, can effectively measure the mass composition of cosmic rays across the Galactic-to-extragalactic transition energy range, leveraging proven radio detection techniques from LOFAR.

title: HI Galaxy Science with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/JingWang01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: This chapter introduces the contributions of the HI galaxy science in this volume reviewing the latest developments and urgent questions in HI galaxy science, providing guiding principles for a layered set of future key science projects. The key science will include: a complete censuses of HI morphologies and kinematics at sub-kpc and 1 km/s resolution within and around galaxies in the nearby Universe; a measurement of the cosmic HI mass density and HI mass function evolution at least up to z~1; an improved understanding of the Universe at z>1, particularly the balance between cold molecular and cool atomic gas. We also provide a view of the synergistic multi-wavelength surveys available in 2028+ in the southern hemisphere. This effort will improve our understanding of the baryon cycle across a significant fraction of the cosmic history, including the processes of gas accretion, consumption and removal as well as AGN and star formation feedback. Based on these science goals, the earlier proposed three-tiered survey strategy remains, but survey parameters and predictions are adjusted according to AA* and AA4 developments. This chapter is an update of the earlier "Advancing Astrophysics with the Square Kilometre Array" chapter 'HI Science with the SKA' by Staveley-Smith & Oosterloo.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews the latest developments and key science goals for HI galaxy science with the SKA, including censuses of HI morphologies and kinematics, measurements of cosmic HI density evolution up to z~1, and understanding gas balance at z>1, with an updated survey strategy based on AA* and AA4 developments.
AI.motivation: To advance understanding of the baryon cycle across cosmic history, including gas accretion, consumption, removal, and feedback processes from star formation and AGN, by leveraging HI galaxy science with the Square Kilometre Array (SKA).
AI.method: A three-tiered survey strategy is proposed, with survey parameters and predictions adjusted based on AA* and AA4 developments, complemented by synergistic multi-wavelength surveys available in 2028+ in the southern hemisphere.
AI.result: Key science outcomes include: complete censuses of HI morphologies and kinematics at sub-kpc and 1 km/s resolution; measurement of cosmic HI mass density and HI mass function evolution up to z~1; improved understanding of cold molecular and cool atomic gas balance at z>1.
AI.conclusion: The updated survey strategy will improve understanding of the baryon cycle across a significant fraction of cosmic history, building upon the earlier SKA HI Science chapter by Staveley-Smith & Oosterloo.

title: Unveiling the roles of thermal and nonthermal processes in the ISM & IGM structure formation and evolution of galaxies with SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2026.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Tabatabaei01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Investigating the thermal and nonthermal processes in the interstellar medium (ISM) and intergalactic medium (IGM) is vital to understanding the evolution of galaxies over cosmic time. Resolved observations with SKA pathfinders show that the nonthermal processes, in which magnetic fields and cosmic rays are involved, can decelerate the formation of massive stars in strongly magnetized regions in nearby galaxies. They can also contribute to the onset of winds and outflows in galaxies. The effects of these processes are stronger at higher redshifts as a result of star formation activities. The SKA Observatory will allow a major breakthrough by mapping the thermal and nonthermal processes in distant universe galaxies, shedding light on the role of the ISM and IGM in the evolution of galaxies. We demonstrate this by simulating the radio continuum and HI emission from local galaxies back to high redshifts. Our simulations show that the AA4 surveys will make it possible to trace the thermal and nonthermal processes of the ISM in galaxies that are analogs to M51 and NGC6946, traced in continuum beyond cosmic noon (z=2-3) and the gas content traced by HI beyond z=1. Both simulations and precursor observations indicate the importance of nonthermal feedback at cosmic noon.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates thermal and nonthermal processes (magnetic fields, cosmic rays) in the ISM and IGM and their role in galaxy evolution. Using simulations of radio continuum and HI emission from local to high-redshift galaxies, the authors show that SKA's AA4 surveys can trace these processes beyond cosmic noon (z=2-3) for continuum and beyond z=1 for HI, highlighting the importance of nonthermal feedback at cosmic noon.
AI.motivation: Understanding how thermal and nonthermal processes (magnetic fields, cosmic rays) in the ISM and IGM influence galaxy evolution across cosmic time is vital but poorly understood, especially at high redshifts.
AI.method: Simulations of radio continuum and HI emission from local galaxies projected to high redshifts, combined with SKA precursor observations, to assess the detectability of thermal and nonthermal ISM processes.
AI.result: SKA's AA4 surveys can trace thermal/nonthermal processes in analogs of M51 and NGC6946 in continuum beyond z=2-3 and HI beyond z=1. Nonthermal feedback is significant at cosmic noon.
AI.conclusion: SKA Observatory will enable a major breakthrough in mapping thermal and nonthermal ISM/IGM processes in distant galaxies, revealing their role in galaxy evolution, particularly nonthermal feedback at cosmic noon.

title: Unveiling a cosmic tango: Integral field spectroscopy and numerical simulations of Arp 143's interaction
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 34 pages, 32 figures
summary: We present spectral data cubes of the interacting galaxy system Arp 143, composed of the ring galaxy NGC 2445 and the lenticular galaxy NGC 2444, obtained with the imaging Fourier transform spectrometer SITELLE at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope. Our data allow to probe the kinematics of the interaction and the chemical properties of the ionized gas. Star-forming regions are almost exclusively found in the ring and nucleus of NGC 2445 with the exception of a few very faint ones discovered at the base of the long tidal plume extending north of NGC 2444. Analysis of the Hα velocity map reveals strong non-circular flows in the ring of NGC 2445, which is expanding. Its nucleus is off-centered with respect to the ring. Oxygen abundance in the ring is on average slightly sub-solar whereas it is close to solar in the nucleus. Broad-band images obtained with the Dragonfly Telephoto array allow to identify the tenuous stellar counterpart of the radio tidal plume. The interaction between the two galaxies is simulated with a chemodynamical evolution code; these simulations suggest that Arp 143 has resulted from a head-on collision between a S0 and a Sc spiral galaxy following a flyby encounter that triggered the formation of the long plume from debris of the disk galaxy.

AI.tldr: This study presents SITELLE spectral data cubes of the interacting galaxy system Arp 143 (NGC 2445 ring galaxy + NGC 2444 lenticular galaxy), revealing kinematics, chemical properties, and star formation distribution. The ring of NGC 2445 shows expanding non-circular flows and an off-centered nucleus; oxygen abundance is slightly sub-solar in the ring and near-solar in the nucleus. Dragonfly images reveal the stellar counterpart of the radio tidal plume. Chemodynamical simulations suggest Arp 143 formed from a head-on collision between an S0 and a Sc spiral galaxy after a flyby encounter that produced the long plume from disk debris.
AI.motivation: To probe the kinematics and chemical properties of the ionized gas in the interacting galaxy system Arp 143, and to understand the interaction history between NGC 2445 (ring galaxy) and NGC 2444 (lenticular galaxy).
AI.method: Imaging Fourier transform spectroscopy (SITELLE at CFHT) for spectral data cubes, broad-band imaging (Dragonfly Telephoto Array) for stellar tidal features, and chemodynamical evolution simulations to model the interaction.
AI.result: Star-forming regions are mostly in the ring and nucleus of NGC 2445, with a few faint ones at the base of the northern tidal plume. Hα velocity maps show strong non-circular expanding flows in the ring; the nucleus is off-centered. Oxygen abundance is slightly sub-solar in the ring and near-solar in the nucleus. The stellar counterpart of the radio tidal plume is identified.
AI.conclusion: Arp 143 likely resulted from a head-on collision between an S0 galaxy (NGC 2444) and a Sc spiral galaxy (NGC 2445) after a flyby encounter, with the long plume formed from disk debris of the spiral galaxy.

title: Start of orbit librations and the bar growth timescale
comment: 13 pages, 12 figures
summary: We study a dynamical model of the Galaxy with an analytical bar that reproduces the radial velocity $V_R$ profiles as a function of the Galactocentric distance $R$ obtained from the Gaia DR3 data. The model radial velocity profiles show a periodic increase in $V_R$ caused by orbits trapped into libration near the outer Lindblad resonance (OLR). To determine the moment when the librations start, we built a set of additional models differing only in the bar growth time $T_g$. The temporal dependences of the radial velocity $V_R$ in the models with different $T_g$ retain their shape but are shifted relative to each other in time $t$. The shift providing the best agreement between the model dependences is proportional to $T_g$ with the coefficient $k = 0.54 \pm 0.02$. Orbit librations do not start when the bar reaches its full strength, but when it attains only 54% of its maximum strength. Since the maximum bar strength in the models is $Q_b = 0.314$, the librations start when the bar strength reaches $Q_b = 0.170$.

AI.tldr: A dynamical Galaxy model with an analytical bar reproduces Gaia DR3 radial velocity profiles. Orbital librations near the outer Lindblad resonance begin when the bar reaches 54% of its maximum strength (Q_b = 0.170), not at full strength.
AI.motivation: To determine when orbit librations near the outer Lindblad resonance begin in a dynamical model of the Galaxy with an evolving bar, by comparing radial velocity profiles from models with different bar growth times to Gaia DR3 data.
AI.method: Built a dynamical Galaxy model with an analytical bar; constructed additional models varying only the bar growth time T_g; analyzed temporal dependences of radial velocity V_R; measured the time shift that provides best agreement between model V_R curves; derived the coefficient k relating shift to T_g.
AI.result: The time shift between V_R curves is proportional to T_g with coefficient k = 0.54 ± 0.02, meaning librations begin when the bar reaches 54% of its maximum strength (Q_b = 0.170), not at full strength (Q_b = 0.314).
AI.conclusion: Orbit librations near the outer Lindblad resonance in Galactic bar models commence at a threshold bar strength of ~54% of the maximum, corresponding to Q_b ≈ 0.170, rather than when the bar is fully grown.

title: Probing Anomalous Microwave Emission with the Square Kilometre Array
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII(AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Vidal01
summary: Anomalous microwave emission (AME) represents an excess of radiation in the 10-60 GHz range, distinct from synchrotron, free-free, or thermal dust emission. Although most commonly attributed to electric dipole radiation from rapidly rotating small dust grains (spinning dust), alternative mechanisms such as magnetic dipole emission (MDE) remain plausible. The detection of AME across diverse environments, from diffuse interstellar clouds to protoplanetary disks and external galaxies, suggests that multiple physical processes or carriers may contribute to its origin. Understanding AME is essential for both Galactic astrophysics and cosmology, as it constitutes a significant foreground for cosmic microwave background (CMB) studies, potentially biasing measurements. This chapter reviews current theoretical frameworks and observational evidence for AME, highlighting the key outstanding questions concerning its emission mechanisms, carriers, and polarization properties. We discuss how the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO), through its unprecedented sensitivity, angular resolution, and frequency coverage, will transform AME studies. SKA observations will enable detailed mapping of AME morphology, precise characterisation of its spectral energy distribution, and the identification of its carriers in Galactic and extragalactic environments. By combining SKA-mid data with higher-frequency observations from ALMA and other facilities such as SPHEREx, it will be possible to disentangle competing models and exploit AME as a diagnostic probe of interstellar grain physics and the small-scale structure of the interstellar medium.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews anomalous microwave emission (AME), an excess radiation in the 10-60 GHz range, discussing its proposed mechanisms (spinning dust vs. magnetic dipole emission), observational status across various environments, and its importance as a CMB foreground. It highlights how the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) will transform AME studies through high sensitivity, resolution, and frequency coverage, enabling carrier identification and model discrimination when combined with ALMA and SPHEREx.
AI.motivation: AME is a significant foreground for CMB studies that can bias measurements; understanding its origin is essential for both Galactic astrophysics and cosmology. Multiple physical processes or carriers may contribute, but key questions about emission mechanisms, carriers, and polarization properties remain unresolved.
AI.method: The paper reviews current theoretical frameworks (spinning dust, magnetic dipole emission) and observational evidence for AME. It discusses how SKAO, combined with ALMA and SPHEREx, will enable detailed morphological mapping, spectral energy distribution characterization, and carrier identification in Galactic and extragalactic environments.
AI.result: AME is detected across diverse environments (diffuse clouds, protoplanetary disks, external galaxies). SKAO's unprecedented capabilities will transform AME studies, and combining SKA-mid with higher-frequency data from ALMA and SPHEREx will allow disentangling competing models.
AI.conclusion: AME can be exploited as a diagnostic probe of interstellar grain physics and the small-scale structure of the interstellar medium once competing models are resolved through multi-facility observations.

title: HALO II: Constraining Hubble constant $H_{0}$ through continuum delay fitting of Fairall 9
comment: Submitted to A&A, 19 pages, 11 figures, and 2 tables
summary: The Hubble tension remains one of the most significant unresolved problems in modern cosmology. A key question is whether it may arise from underestimated systematic uncertainties in the different measurement techniques. In this context, new independent methods are of exceptional importance. We therefore pursue a novel approach to determining the Hubble constant, $H_{0}$ based on continuum time delay and spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling in active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Unlike conventional techniques, this method is entirely independent of the cosmic distance ladder and does not require cross-calibration against other distance indicators. As a result, it enables a direct determination of $H_{0}$, free from the arbitrary normalizations that often affect indirect measurements. We conducted a dedicated monitoring campaign of the Seyfert galaxy Fairall 9 and further developed the {\tt H0RIZON-AGN} model to interpret the resulting observations. The model incorporates the effects of radiation reprocessing in the surrounding cold accretion disk, enabling a more realistic description of the observed continuum delays. Through the simultaneous modeling of the continuum lag-spectrum and the broadband SED of Fairall 9, we derived a Hubble constant of $H_{0}=72.4_{-3.7}^{+3.4} \, \rm km \, s^{-1} \, Mpc^{-1}$. title: 3D Magnetic Field Vectors in Space: Bubbles, Clouds, and Filaments
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Tahani01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes. 30 pages, 5 figures
summary: Magnetic fields play important roles in the star-formation process across different spatial scales. The interplay between magnetic field strength (a key component of the interstellar medium's energy budget) and field orientation relative to density structures impacts how interstellar material evolves toward star formation. To understand galactic evolution toward stars, planets, and ultimately life, we need to map three-dimensional (3D) magnetic field vectors in 3D space. However, determining full vector information remains challenging due to projection effects and the complex relationship between observable tracers and field geometry. We outline the observational techniques that can be used to probe the 3D magnetic field structures of objects such as supernova remnants (SNR), superbubbles, HII regions, and HI filaments in the diffuse interstellar medium (ISM), and objects in the dense ISM such as molecular clouds, filaments, and cores. The main SKA-specific observational techniques include synchrotron emission and Faraday rotation of both compact sources and the diffuse emission. We discuss how SKA AA4 will allow implementation of the techniques we describe, leveraging the vastly improved sensitivity, resolution and uv-coverage compared to existing datasets. This will enhance our ability to reconstruct 3D magnetic field vectors, advancing our understanding of magnetic fields in Galactic evolution and star formation.
